prompt.context: Your client, NASA, has recently learned of a giant asteroid heading towards the Earth. Scientists at NASA have determined that there is a 10 percent probability that this asteroid makes landfall. If it hits, the asteroid will create a large dust storm blocking out sunlight and preventing photosynthesis in plants. This will ultimately destroy the rest of the earth's ecosystem for the next 100 years. NASA needs help determining whether they should launch the Eternity Mission, a space exploration mission to find a suitable planet for the human population to live on in the event of the catastrophic asteroid impact.
prompt.question: Should NASA launch the Eternity Mission? If so, which planet(s) should be explored, and which planet should be visited first?

clarifying_info.q: What is NASA's goal for the evacuation?
clarifying_info.a: NASA's goal is to safely evacuate at least 20% of the world's population in the event of impact.

clarifying_info.q: What is the timeline for the asteroid impact and evacuation?
clarifying_info.a: The asteroid would hit earth in 25 years. NASA estimates it will require 15 years to build enough space vehicles and safely evacuate 20% of the world's population. Therefore, Mission Eternity needs to be completed within 10 years.

clarifying_info.q: How fast can NASA's spacecraft travel?
clarifying_info.a: Assume NASA has had major breakthroughs in space travel and spacecraft can now travel at the speed of light.

clarifying_info.q: Can other international space agencies contribute budget?
clarifying_info.a: Other international space agencies are looking to NASA to make a decision. Their budgets are unavailable to aid this mission.

clarifying_info.q: Has NASA considered other options to save the population?
clarifying_info.a: NASA has already weighed other options such as hitting the asteroid to break it into smaller pieces, and determined that is not possible. Other efforts to live underground are being researched separately.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of the Eternity Mission?
clarifying_info.a: Cost of the Eternity Mission will vary by planet(s) selected for exploration; specific figures are not available.

clarifying_info.q: How will astronauts survive very long space travel?
clarifying_info.a: Assume NASA has figured out a way to use therapeutic hypothermia hibernation to enable humans to travel very long distances in space.

exhibits.title: Distance from Earth to Candidate Planets
exhibits.shows: A diagram showing Earth and four potentially habitable planets (W, X, Y, Z) with their respective distances from Earth in trillions of miles.

exhibits.title: Planet Habitability Indicators
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot comparing Planet X, Planet Y, and Planet Z on two axes: Earth Similarity Index (ESI, scale 0.0 to 1.0) and Percentile Location in Habitable Zone (0 to 100).
exhibits.data: Planet Y: ESI ~0.8, Habitable Zone ~80th percentile; Planet Z: ESI ~0.6, Habitable Zone ~60th percentile; Planet X: ESI ~0.4, Habitable Zone ~40th percentile

framework: Budget Issues: Cost of spacecraft, fuel (renewable technology), astronaut salaries/life insurance/training, ground staff, tracking device upkeep, cost of test runs; consider outside fundraising from businesses, nonprofits, donations
Timing Issues: Distance to potential planet, duration of project affecting cost, timing of receiving planet data before asteroid impact deadline
Public Relations / Liability: Public response to expense, public reaction to disaster if mission accident occurs, loss of credibility for future missions and existing projects if there is a failure
Available Planet Data: Accuracy of currently available data regarding potential planets, determining which metrics to prioritize

questions.prompt: Given the 10-year deadline, which planets can NASA realistically explore and receive data from in time?
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert distances from trillions of miles to light-years (1 light-year = 6 trillion miles), add 18 months (1.5 years) for on-site data collection, and add the data signal travel time (3 months per light-year = 0.25 years per light-year). Candidate should conclude Planet W exceeds the 10-year window and must be eliminated. Planets X, Y, and Z all return data within 10 years.

math.setup: 1 light-year = 6 trillion miles. Data collection = 1.5 years. Signal travel time = 0.25 years per light-year of distance. Total time = (distance in light-years) + 1.5 + (distance in light-years x 0.25).
steps: Planet W: 48 / 6 = 8 light-years travel; signal = 8 x 0.25 = 2 years; total = 8 + 1.5 + 2 = 11.5 years — EXCEEDS 10-year limit
Planet X: 24 / 6 = 4 light-years travel; signal = 4 x 0.25 = 1 year; total = 4 + 1.5 + 1 = 6.5 years — within limit
Planet Y: 36 / 6 = 6 light-years travel; signal = 6 x 0.25 = 1.5 years; total = 6 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 9 years — within limit
Planet Z: 33 / 6 = 5.5 light-years travel; signal = 5.5 x 0.25 = 1.375 years; total = 5.5 + 1.5 + 1.375 = 8.375 years — within limit
math.answer: Planet W is eliminated (11.5 years > 10-year deadline). Viable planets: X (6.5 yrs), Z (8.375 yrs), Y (9 yrs).

questions.prompt: What metrics would you want to look at when comparing Planets X, Y, and Z to determine which is most suitable to sustain human life?
questions.guidance: Strong answers organize brainstorm into clear buckets: distance/travel feasibility, food/water availability, atmospheric conditions, natural resources, and climate. Candidate should proactively ask for available data on these dimensions before proceeding to Exhibit 2.

questions.prompt: Given the habitability data in Exhibit 2, which planet should NASA visit?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read Exhibit 2 and identify Planet Y as having the highest Earth Similarity Index (~0.8) and the highest percentile location in the habitable zone (~80th percentile), making it the best candidate to support human life. NASA only has the manpower and financial resources to visit one planet; Planet Y has the best indicators. Candidate should note that in astronomy, the habitable zone indicates likelihood of liquid water, and ESI measures physical similarity to Earth on a 0-to-1 scale.

brainstorming.prompt: How should NASA determine which planet to explore first? What metrics would you want to look at when comparing Planets X, Y, and Z?

categories.name: Distance from Earth
ideas: Feasibility of transferring population with less risk
Space travel timing issues — shorter distance means faster round-trip and data return

categories.name: Food and Water
ideas: Ability to raise livestock and sources of protein

categories.name: Atmospheric Conditions
ideas: Air quality — is it breathable or does it require a head mask?

categories.name: Natural Resources
ideas: Geography — buildable terrain, safety of terrain

recommendation: NASA should launch the Eternity Mission to Planet Y because it will return data before the 10-year deadline (9 years total) and has the highest indicators to sustain human life — with an ESI of approximately 0.8 and a location in the 80th percentile of a habitable zone.
risks: Planet Y is the furthest of the viable options from Earth, making the trip and hibernation riskier for astronauts.
The longer journey is also more costly and consumes a higher proportion of NASA's annual budget.
A 10% asteroid impact probability means there is a 90% chance the mission may not ultimately be needed.
next_steps: Prepare and launch the Eternity Mission to Planet Y.
Depending on available budget and resources, consider launching a parallel or follow-on mission to Planet Z, which would still return data in time (8.375 years) and serves as a backup option.
Begin parallel planning for spacecraft construction needed to evacuate 20% of the world's population, to ensure the 15-year build timeline can begin immediately upon receipt of planet data.
